one_liner: Java FFM bindings to Linux io_uring (via liburing) for batched file reads/writes; beats FileChannel on small random reads.
what_it_does: JUring exposes io_uring's submission/completion model to Java: you create a ring (new JUring(queueDepth, flags...)), queue operations with prepareRead/prepareWrite/prepareOpen/prepareClose (plus readv/writev, fixed-buffer variants and, since May 2026, accept/connect/recv/send), call submit(), then reap Result records with peekForBatchResult/waitForBatchResult/waitForResult. Operations target raw int fds or registered-file indexes, and read data comes back in native MemorySegments. JUringBlocking wraps a ring with a poller thread and returns a CompletableFuture per operation for blocking-style code on virtual threads. It is not a FileChannel replacement; an io_uring FileChannel exists only in an unmerged third-party fork (issue #34).
how_it_is_fast: Batching: the benchmark loop keeps up to 256 reads in flight per thread, submits every 64 SQEs with one io_uring_submit, and reaps completions in bulk with io_uring_peek_batch_cqe + io_uring_cq_advance. FileChannel does one pread-style syscall per call. Registered files (io_uring_register_files + IOSQE_FIXED_FILE) and optional registered buffers (read_fixed/write_fixed) cut per-op fd and buffer setup. Calls go through Java FFM downcalls into liburing-ffi.so, with hot functions (get_sqe, set_flags, submit, cqe_seen, cq_advance) marked Linker.Option.critical. Per-op user_data structs come from a malloc-backed pool ('ZeroGc' classes) and buffers are native, so the hot path avoids GC allocation.
when_to_use: JVM service on Linux issuing many small random reads (512B-4KB) against a fixed set of files that can be opened once and registered with the ring (README: +55% at 512B, +489% at 4KB at 25 threads).
Code that can batch: tens to hundreds of operations in flight per thread, one submit per batch, completions reaped in bulk.
Single-threaded or lightly threaded writers (README: +123% to +246% at 1 thread, +33% to +77% at 8 threads below 64KB).
Workloads that open, read and close many files, where io_uring openat/close can be queued too (README: +13% to +48% vs FileChannel open/read/close).
Blocking-style code on virtual threads that wants io_uring reads behind a Future (README: +14% to +138% vs FileChannel on virtual threads).
when_not_to_use: Many concurrent writers or large writes: at 20 threads JUring ties at 512B and loses 2%, 16% and 33% at 4KB, 16KB and 64KB, and at 8 threads it loses 3% at 64KB.
One synchronous operation at a time: the gain comes from batching. In issue #34 a fork's 'JUring sync' took 0.68 ms vs 0.26 ms for standard O_DIRECT FileChannel on a 10-page write.
Portability: Linux only, needs liburing >= 2.4 installed (liburing-ffi.so), and pom.xml targets JDK 25.

You need a drop-in NIO API (FileChannel, AsynchronousFileChannel, ByteBuffer) or a supported artifact: it is 0.1-SNAPSHOT, has no releases, is not on Maven Central, has no CI config in the repo, and the README lists 'Simplicity (Working on this!)'.
Code that cannot manage native memory by hand: read/recv buffers are malloc'd and leak unless freeBuffer()/close() is called.

integration.form: source-drop (Maven project with JPMS module 'JUring', 0.1-SNAPSHOT; build the jar yourself, no published artifact)
integration.dependencies: liburing >= 2.4 on the host (loads liburing-ffi.so; FFI support arrived in liburing 2.4) and libc; no runtime Java dependencies (JMH, JUnit, AssertJ are test-scope)
integration.min_toolchain: JDK 25 per pom.xml (README says Java 22+); run with --enable-native-access; Linux kernel 5.1+ per README, 5.19+ for multishot accept, 6.0/6.1+ for the SINGLE_ISSUER/DEFER_TASKRUN flags the benchmarks use
integration.platforms: Linux only; pure Java over FFM, so any arch with liburing-ffi (the devcontainer is arm64 Ubuntu 25.04); the benchmark machine is undocumented
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. From source: a JUring instance is single-threaded (unsynchronized user_data pool and buffer stack), and the benchmarks use one ring per thread. In JUringBlocking the caller thread checks slots out of the same unsynchronized pool that its poller thread checks them back into, so concurrent use looks racy (inferred, not tested).

gotchas: Errors are not thrown. Each Result carries the raw CQE result, so check for a negative errno yourself. Issue #17: a write on a read-only fd 'passes silently'; the maintainer closed it and left the check to callers. The benchmarks also count completions without checking results.

Ring capacity is not guarded: getSqe checks for Java null, but an FFM downcall returns MemorySegment.NULL. Queuing more than queueDepth operations before submit() likely hands liburing a NULL SQE and crashes the JVM (inferred from source).
JUringBlocking starts a platform poller thread per instance. With the default timeout it spins on Thread.yield(), which burns a core; the benchmark sets a 1 ms sleep instead.
The Java code hardcodes liburing's struct io_uring layout (LibUringDispatcher), so a liburing build with a different struct layout could break it; the tested liburing versions are not documented.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick JUring only when you must stay on the JVM and your bottleneck is file I/O through FileChannel. The catalogued siblings (Condy, the Asio io_uring backend, monoio, uring_exec) are more mature native C++/Rust io_uring runtimes built mainly for network event loops, so in native code use them instead.
verified_claims_summary: These are first-party JMH results on an unnamed Linux machine; CPU, storage, kernel, JDK and JVM flags are not stated. For reads, 25 threads do buffered (not O_DIRECT) random reads over 2,211 files of 5 MiB each. JUring uses registered files with up to 256 in flight per thread; the FileChannel baseline does one synchronous read at a time into a new heap ByteBuffer. Results: +55% at 512B, +489% at 4KB, +23%/+16% at 16KB/64KB. The 4KB point implies about 55 GB/s, about 4x JUring's byte rate at other sizes, so it looks like a page-cache outlier. Writes (O_DIRECT in the current bench code) gain +123% to +246% single-threaded but lose up to 33% at 20 threads.
status_note: Active (socket support and readv merged May 2026, last commit 2026-05-07) but pre-release: 0.1-SNAPSHOT with no tags, no Maven Central artifact and no CI. The Unlicense public-domain dedication (no patent grant) makes its 80 main-source Java files easy to vendor.
